nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests security, reliability and fewer crashes, so developers use it to praise a language or tool.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers use this term constantly in security and language discussions, especially about Rust, Go and Java compared with C and C++. Put the hyphen before a noun ('a memory-safe language') and leave it out after a verb ('the language is memory safe'). Outside tech, the phrase would sound odd.

distinctions.note: Type safety prevents misusing values as the wrong type, while memory safety specifically prevents invalid reads and writes of memory; the two often overlap.
Secure is broader and covers authentication, encryption and configuration, while memory-safe describes only one class of language guarantees.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in software says Rust is memory-safe, which is why she likes it so much.
examples.professional: We are rewriting the image parser in a memory-safe language to eliminate an entire class of buffer overflow bugs.
examples.analytical: A memory-safe language guarantees through its type system and runtime checks that a program never reads or writes memory it does not own.

nuance.analogy: Memory-safe is like a seatbelt for code: it does not stop every accident, but it prevents many of the worst crashes.
nuance.etymology: Compound of memory (from Latin memoria) and safe (from Latin salvus, meaning whole or unharmed).
common_mistakes: Leaving out the hyphen before a noun, or writing 'memory safe language' without it.
Treating memory-safe as meaning fully secure, when it only addresses certain kinds of memory bugs.

senses.definition: A collection of live wild animals as an exhibition historically associated with the aristocracy and considered a precursor of modern zoos.
senses.example: The eighteenth-century duke kept a menagerie of lions, bears, and exotic birds at his estate.

senses.definition: The enclosure where they are kept.
senses.example: Visitors gathered at the menagerie's iron railings to watch the tigers pace.

senses.definition: A diverse or miscellaneous group.
senses.example: Our hiking club is a menagerie of retirees, students, and software engineers.

senses.definition: The orchestra of a theater.
senses.example: The theater's menagerie tuned their instruments in the pit before the curtain rose.

core.definition: A collection of wild or exotic animals kept for display; also, any varied or odd group of people or things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NAJ. The final "-ie" is pronounced "ree", and the middle "-er-" is a reduced "uh".

nuance.connotation: Neutral, sometimes humorous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use menagerie for animal collections in parks or private homes, and often in a playful way for a group of odd or quirky people. Saying "This office is a menagerie" is a friendly comment. It sounds old-fashioned for a modern zoo, where Americans usually say zoo.

distinctions.note: A zoo is a modern, organized public institution; a menagerie is an older or informal collection of animals.
Collection is neutral and general; menagerie suggests a varied, sometimes chaotic mix of creatures or people.

examples.everyday: My sister's house is a menagerie with two dogs, a cat, and three fish.
examples.professional: Our team is a menagerie of backgrounds, from statisticians to former designers, which keeps our meetings interesting.
examples.analytical: Early modern European courts maintained royal menageries as displays of power, which later evolved into public zoos.

nuance.analogy: A menagerie is like a box of mixed crayons: many different colors and types, all gathered in one place.
nuance.etymology: From French ménagerie, from ménage, household, from Latin mansio-related roots.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable.
Using menagerie as a synonym for zoo in formal American writing; zoo is the standard term.

menagerie.etymology: From French *ménagerie*, derived from *ménager* (“to keep house”), *ménage*.

senses.definition: A mindset; a way of thinking; a set of beliefs.
senses.example: Before he can succeed, he will have to shed the mentality that he can get by without hard work.

senses.definition: The characteristics of a mind described as a system of distinctive structures and processes based in biology, language, or culture, etc. a mental system.
senses.example: The startup's mentality of constant experimentation shaped every decision it made.

core.definition: A habitual way of thinking; a set of attitudes and beliefs that shapes how someone sees situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAL. The middle syllable is a reduced 'uh', and the final 'ity' is pronounced 'uh-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral by default; it becomes negative with words like 'siege mentality' or 'us-versus-them mentality'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mentality' often in business, sports, politics, and everyday discussion of attitudes, as in 'a winning mentality'. It is neutral but can sound critical when it describes a narrow or fixed way of thinking. 'Mindset' is a close and very common American alternative.

distinctions.note: Mindset is the more common American word in business and self-help talk. Mentality is slightly more formal and can carry a stronger sense of group attitude.
Attitude is a feeling or position toward something in a particular moment. Mentality is deeper and more habitual.

examples.everyday: My coach says we need a winning mentality if we want to beat that team.
examples.professional: Our product team needs a customer-first mentality when we plan the next release.
examples.analytical: Weber traced how a religious mentality shaped the economic habits of early capitalism.

nuance.analogy: A mentality is like the default setting on a computer: it runs in the background and shapes what happens next.
nuance.etymology: From French mentalité, from Medieval Latin mentalitas, from mentalis, mental.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'mental', the adjective. You can say 'a mental state' but 'a state of mentality' sounds unusual.
Using it for simple thoughts. It refers to a habitual pattern, not one idea.

senses.definition: In a merciful manner.
Thankfully.

core.definition: Thankfully, as a relief; or in a kind, merciful way toward someone who is suffering or at fault.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and say it as four syllables. The '-ful' reduces to a short 'fuh', and the final '-ly' is light, so avoid 'mer-SIFF-ly'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It signals relief and kindness, and it suggests that something bad was avoided or ended.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use mercifully as a sentence adverb meaning 'thankfully', usually at the start of a sentence: 'Mercifully, the rain stopped.' It can also mean 'kindly' in a more formal sense, as in a sermon or a news report about a rescue. In casual talk, 'thankfully' or 'luckily' is more common.

distinctions.note: Thankfully is a neutral marker of relief, while mercifully adds a sense that something painful or dreadful has been avoided or ended.
Luckily stresses chance, while mercifully suggests a kind or merciful outcome, often after suffering.

examples.everyday: Mercifully, the traffic cleared up, so we made it to the airport on time.
examples.professional: Mercifully, the client accepted the revised timeline, so the release did not slip again.
examples.analytical: Mercifully, the author avoids a simple moral verdict, letting the reader feel the suffering without turning it into a lesson.

nuance.analogy: Like finding an umbrella just as the storm starts: the trouble is still there, but you were spared its worst part.
nuance.etymology: From merciful plus -ly; mercy comes from Old French merci, from Latin merces (reward, wages).
common_mistakes: Using mercifully as a noun meaning 'mercy' or 'kindness'; it is an adverb.
Stressing the '-ful' syllable, as in 'mer-si-FUL-ly'; the stress is on the first syllable.

senses.definition: That is the ratio of two holomorphic functions (and so possibly infinite at a discrete set of points).
senses.example: Our complex analysis exam asked whether the function f(z)=1/(z-2) is meromorphic on the entire plane.

core.definition: Of a complex function: holomorphic everywhere except at isolated poles, so it can be written as a ratio of two holomorphic functions.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MOR, in the middle of the word, and the 'o' in 'mero' is a diphthong 'oh'. Keep the r clear in both syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in complex analysis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'meromorphic' only in mathematics, especially complex analysis and graduate courses. In conversation, mathematicians would say 'a function with poles' or 'holomorphic except at poles' when they want a plainer phrase. Outside technical settings, the word would sound very specialized.

distinctions.note: A holomorphic function is complex differentiable at every point of its domain; a meromorphic function may fail to be holomorphic at isolated poles.
Analytic is a broader term in complex analysis; meromorphic specifically allows isolated poles.

examples.everyday: My math homework asked whether a certain function was meromorphic, and I still am not sure what that means.
examples.professional: The simulation model assumes the transfer function is meromorphic, so its poles determine the system's stability.
examples.analytical: A function that is meromorphic on the whole complex plane can be expressed as a quotient of entire functions, which clarifies the role of its poles.

nuance.analogy: Like a smooth road with a few potholes that are isolated and countable: the road is mostly fine, but the holes are places where it breaks.
nuance.etymology: From Greek meros, 'part', and morphē, 'form', with the -ic suffix; the term refers to functions that are mostly holomorphic.
common_mistakes: Confusing meromorphic with 'homomorphic', which is a term from algebra.
Forgetting that poles are isolated points, not whole regions where the function fails.

senses.definition: An elementary particle that is composed of a quark and an antiquark, such as a kaon or pion. (Mesons composed of rarer quarks are much heavier.)
The mesial plane dividing the body into similar right and left halves.
senses.example: The surgeon marked the meson of the skull before making the incision along the midline.

core.definition: An subatomic particle made of one quark and one antiquark, such as a pion or kaon, that carries the strong nuclear force between particles.

pronunciation.tip: In the physics sense, stress the first syllable and use a long e, MEE-zahn, not MESS-on. Do not confuse it with the anatomical word mesial, MEE-zee-ul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise scientific term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Physicists use meson in particle physics, especially when discussing collisions at accelerators such as the LHC. Most non-specialists will not need it, but it appears in science news and textbooks. Americans say the full name of a specific meson, such as pion or kaon, when precision matters.

distinctions.note: A baryon is made of three quarks, such as a proton or neutron, while a meson is made of one quark and one antiquark.
A lepton, such as an electron, does not feel the strong nuclear force, whereas a meson does.

examples.everyday: I have no idea what a meson is, but my nephew keeps talking about them after his physics class.
examples.professional: The detector logged a neutral pion, a type of meson, in the collision data from last night's run.
examples.analytical: A meson is not a fundamental building block but a bound state whose properties reveal how the strong force holds quarks together.

nuance.analogy: A meson is like a two-person dance team: one partner is a quark and the other an antiquark, bound tightly together.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mesos, middle, because its mass was originally found to be between that of the electron and the proton.
common_mistakes: Saying MESS-on, which mixes up the word with the anatomical term mesial.
Confusing meson with baryon, which is made of three quarks, not one quark and one antiquark.

senses.definition: A device that measures things.
senses.example: gas meter

senses.definition: A parking meter or similar device for collecting payment.
senses.example: gas meter

senses.definition: A line above or below a hanging net, to which the net is attached in order to strengthen it.
senses.example: We replaced the frayed meter line along the bottom of the net before the fishing trip.

senses.definition: US standard spelling of meter (“a unit of measure”).
senses.example: The race covers a distance of one hundred meters along the flat track.

senses.definition: US standard spelling of meter (“the rhythm or measure”).
senses.example: The hymn's common meter makes it easy for the congregation to sing from memory.

senses.definition: (dated) One who metes or measures.
senses.example: a laboring coal-meter
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To measure with a metering device.
senses.example: The utility company will meter our water use starting next month.

senses.definition: To imprint a postage mark with a postage meter.
senses.example: The office clerk metered the envelopes before dropping them into the outgoing mail bin.

senses.definition: To regulate the flow of or to deliver in regulated amounts (usually of fluids but sometimes of other things such as anticipation or breath).
senses.example: The pump meters insulin into the bloodstream in small, regulated doses throughout the day.

core.definition: A device that measures and records an amount, such as electricity, water or time; also the metric unit of length.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MEE-. The second syllable is a reduced, r-colored vowel, so avoid saying 'meet-AIR' even though the spelling ends in -er.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word for measuring devices and has no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'meter' constantly for utility meters, parking meters and the unit of length, which appears in running races and the metric system. In American spelling it is always 'meter', even for the unit, while British writers use 'metre'. Ordinary speakers say 'the gas meter' or 'the meter reader' rather than technical terms.

distinctions.note: A gauge shows a current reading on a dial, while a meter often records a running total, like a utility meter.
Metre is the British spelling of the unit of length; in American English the correct spelling is meter.

examples.everyday: I forgot to feed the meter, so I'm going to run out and move the car before I get a ticket.
examples.professional: Field technicians read the smart meters remotely each month, so we no longer need site visits.
examples.analytical: A meter reports only what it is calibrated to detect, so its readings are only as reliable as the calibration behind them.

nuance.analogy: A utility meter is like an odometer for electricity or water: it keeps a running total of what has been used.
nuance.etymology: From Greek metron 'measure'; the device sense comes from the suffix -meter, meaning 'measuring instrument'.
common_mistakes: Spelling the unit of length 'metre', which is British; American writing uses 'meter'.
Using 'meter' as a plain verb without an object; Americans say 'meter out' or 'meter the flow of' instead.

meter.etymology: From Middle English *metere* (“one who measures, measurer”), perhaps from Old English *metend* (“one who measures or metes”), equivalent to *mete* + *-er*.

senses.definition: The field of economics that deals with small-scale economic activities such as those of an individual or company.
senses.example: Her microeconomics course explained how a single bakery sets its prices and wages.

core.definition: The branch of economics that studies the behavior of individual consumers, households, and firms and how they make decisions about prices and resources.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the "NAH" in "economics," not on "eco." The "eco" is pronounced "ek-uh" with a reduced middle vowel, and the final "-ics" is a short "iks."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a field of study and carries no evaluative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in university courses, policy debates, business settings, and news about markets. Economists often contrast it with "macroeconomics," which studies the whole economy. In everyday conversation, people usually just say "economics" or talk about "how the market works" instead.

distinctions.note: Microeconomics studies individual markets, firms and households, while macroeconomics studies the whole economy, such as inflation, unemployment, and GDP.
Economics is the broad field, and microeconomics is one of its two main branches.

examples.everyday: My daughter is taking a microeconomics class this semester, and she says supply and demand finally makes sense to her.
examples.professional: Our pricing model relies on microeconomics, so we need to understand how individual customers respond to a price change.
examples.analytical: Microeconomics assumes rational agents who optimize under constraints, and this assumption shapes how economists model choice.

nuance.analogy: If economics is a whole city map, microeconomics is the street-level view of each block and each shop.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mikros "small" plus "economics," from Greek oikonomia "household management."
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in "MY-kro-eh-kuh-NAH-miks," which makes the word hard to recognize.
Confusing it with "macroeconomics" when talking about whole-country issues like inflation or unemployment.

core.definition: A member of the Midianites, a nomadic desert people descended from Abraham through his son Midian, who appear in the Old Testament as traders and enemies of Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MID. The middle syllable is a weak 'ee-uh', and the final syllable rhymes with 'bite'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a term used in Bible study and history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Midianite mainly in Bible classes, sermons and scholarly discussion of the Old Testament. It can be a noun for a person or an adjective, as in 'the Midianite traders.' It is not used in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Midian is the name of the ancestor and the region; Midianite refers to the people who lived there.

examples.everyday: Our pastor mentioned the Midianites in last Sunday's sermon, and I looked them up afterward.
examples.professional: For the lesson plan, students should compare how the Midianite traders appear in Genesis and in the story of Gideon.
examples.analytical: The Midianite identity in the Hebrew Bible is shaped by the tension between kinship with Israel and their role as enemies, a tension the text handles with care.

nuance.analogy: The Midianites are like a neighboring family in a long feud and a long friendship at once: close enough to be related, but often on the other side of the fence.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Midyan, the name of Abraham's son, with the suffix -ite meaning a member of a group.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying 'mid-ee-AN-ite'; the stress falls on the first syllable.
Using Midianite as a word for any desert nomad; it refers to a specific people in the Bible.
nuance.biblical_note: The Midianites were a people descended from Abraham through Midian, appearing in the Old Testament as traders, herders and raiders. In Genesis 37:28 RSV, Midianite traders draw Joseph out of the pit and he is sold to Ishmaelites who carry him to Egypt, and in Genesis 37:36 the Midianites sell him in Egypt. In Numbers 31 RSV, Israel makes war on the Midianites, and in Judges 6-8 RSV, Gideon defeats Midianite raiders who had oppressed Israel. The Midianites are also mentioned as part of the wider network of desert peoples around Israel.

senses.definition: (historical) A girl or young woman who milks the cows on a farm.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A young woman who milks cows on a farm, a figure now mostly seen in old stories, pictures, and rural history.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MILK, and let the final 'maid' rhyme with 'made'. Do not reduce it to 'mud'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to nostalgic; it suggests rural life and sometimes an idealized, old-fashioned innocence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans now use milkmaid mostly in literature, art history, or nostalgic talk about the past. Modern dairy workers are called dairy farmers, dairy workers, or milkers, and milking is usually done by machine. Do not use the word as a job title for a current employee.

distinctions.note: A dairy farmer is the modern, gender-neutral term for someone who runs a dairy operation; milkmaid is old-fashioned and refers specifically to a young woman.
A milkman delivers milk to homes; a milkmaid milks the cows, so the two words describe different jobs.

examples.everyday: My grandmother kept a porcelain milkmaid figurine on her kitchen windowsill.
examples.professional: Our dairy no longer hires milkmaids; we employ trained technicians who run automated milking systems.
examples.analytical: The milkmaid became a stock figure of rural innocence in eighteenth-century European painting and verse.

nuance.analogy: A milkmaid is like a character in a storybook: vivid and charming, but no longer part of everyday modern work.
nuance.etymology: Compound of milk and maid, meaning a young woman who milks.
common_mistakes: Using milkmaid as a current job title; dairy worker or dairy farmer is the modern term.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'mud' rather than 'mayd'.

senses.definition: The property of being minute.
senses.example: The minuteness of the watch's gears amazed the apprentice, who needed a magnifying loupe to see them.

senses.definition: (rare) Something very tiny.
senses.example: A minuteness of dust had settled on the lens, invisible until the light hit it.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The quality of being extremely small or detailed, so that something is hard to see or measure without close attention.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable. The t is clear and not flapped, and the final -ness is a weak 'nis'. Do not say the first syllable as MIN-it, which is the time unit.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, suggesting precision or difficulty in observing small things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use minuteness mostly in writing or formal description of fine detail, such as in science, art, or engineering reports. In everyday conversation, they usually say 'how tiny' or 'how small.' The word stresses the fine detail rather than general size.

distinctions.note: Smallness is a general word for being little in size; minuteness suggests tiny, detailed features that require close attention.
Tininess is informal and simply means very small; minuteness is more formal and suggests precision.

examples.everyday: I could not see the minuteness of the stitching without my glasses.
examples.professional: The minuteness of the sensor's readings made calibration difficult in the lab.
examples.analytical: The minuteness of the differences between the two models makes any conclusion about superiority fragile.

nuance.analogy: Like the grain of sand in an hourglass, too small to notice alone but essential to the whole.
nuance.etymology: From minute (adjective) plus the suffix -ness, meaning the state or quality of being.
common_mistakes: Using minuteness for the time unit, as in 'a minuteness of waiting'; the time unit is minute, not minuteness.
Stressing the first syllable (MIN-it-ness) as if it were the time unit.

senses.definition: That can be mitigated.
senses.example: The damage from the flood was mitigable if the levees were repaired quickly.

core.definition: Able to be made less severe, reduced, or lessened, though not always completely removed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MIT, and the middle syllables reduce to quick, unstressed vowels. The final -able is pronounced as a reduced bul, not as a full ay-bul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a problem or harm as manageable rather than fixed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mitigable mainly in risk management, law, policy, engineering, and insurance. In everyday talk, people say can be reduced, fixable, or manageable. The word implies that the problem can be made smaller, not necessarily eliminated.

distinctions.note: Curable means a condition can be fully removed, while mitigable means it can only be reduced or lessened.
Fixable is informal and implies complete repair, while mitigable suggests reducing the harm.

examples.everyday: The leak looks bad, but it's mitigable if we shut off the valve now.
examples.professional: The vendor said the outage was mitigable with a rollback and a cache warm-up.
examples.analytical: Whether the harm is mitigable depends on whether the damage is reversible or only reducible.

nuance.analogy: Like a fever: you can bring it down with medicine, but it may not vanish completely.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin mitigabilis, from mitigare, from mitis ('mild') plus agere ('to make').
common_mistakes: Using mitigable to mean completely removable; it means only that the harm can be lessened.
Confusing mitigable (standard) with mitigatable, a less common variant.

senses.definition: To be overprotective and indulgent toward; to pamper.
senses.example: My sister mollycoddles her son, never letting him fix his own mistakes or face any disappointment.

senses.definition: (rare) A person, especially a man or a boy, who is pampered and overprotected.
senses.example: Nobody at the office respected him, since everyone saw him as a spoiled mollycoddle.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To treat someone too gently or protectively, doing things for them that they should learn to do themselves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable MAH and the second syllable KAH. The final syllables are reduced, so the last two sound like 'dul', not 'dawl'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests that the person being coddled is weak or immature, and that the protection is harmful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mollycoddle informally, often for parents, teachers, or bosses who protect people too much. It is often used with a judgment, as in 'Stop mollycoddling him.' It can sound harsh if said directly to someone, so people often use it when talking about a third person. A natural reply is 'You're right, I need to let him figure it out.'

distinctions.note: Pamper means to indulge someone with comfort or luxury and can be positive, while mollycoddle is always critical of overprotection.
Coddle is the same kind of gentle indulgence but is milder and can be affectionate, while mollycoddle is stronger and more disapproving.

examples.everyday: Stop mollycoddling your little brother, he is old enough to tie his own shoes.
examples.professional: We should not mollycoddle junior analysts, because they learn faster when they debug their own code.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that an overly protective welfare system can mollycoddle citizens and weaken their sense of responsibility.

nuance.analogy: To mollycoddle someone is like wrapping a young plant in so much cloth that it never grows strong roots.
nuance.etymology: Nineteenth-century English, combining 'molly' (an effeminate man or boy) with 'coddle' (to pamper).
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'molly coddle' with two words in formal writing.
Using it as a neutral word for gentle care; it is usually critical.
Stressing the final syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: A molt; the shedding of skin, feathers, etc.

core.definition: The process by which an animal periodically sheds its skin, feathers, hair, or shell and grows a new covering.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOHLT-. Pronounce the t clearly before the -ing ending, and don't insert a vowel between the l and t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a natural biological process.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'molting' for birds, insects, crabs, and reptiles, and in pet care for birds and some other animals. For dogs and cats, people normally say 'shedding', which is the everyday word for losing hair. The American spelling is 'molting', not 'moulting'.

distinctions.note: Shedding is the everyday word for losing hair or fur, while molting is the more technical term for losing feathers, skin, or shells.
Ecdysis is a technical term for molting in arthropods such as insects and crabs, used mainly in science.

examples.everyday: Our chickens are molting right now, so they aren't laying eggs.
examples.professional: The lab tracks molting in the crab colony so we can schedule the feeding trials around it.
examples.analytical: Molting in arthropods requires building a new exoskeleton beneath the old one before shedding it, which leaves the animal vulnerable for a time.

nuance.analogy: Like a snake sloughing off a skin that no longer fits, molting replaces an outer covering that has outgrown its use.
nuance.etymology: From molt, from Middle English moulten, from Old English mūtian 'to exchange', from Latin mutare 'to change'.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling 'moulting' in American writing.
Saying 'I am molting' for human hair loss, which sounds odd to Americans.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or being a monad.
Having an arity of one (taking a single argument or operand)
senses.example: "The monadic existential quantifier ∃, as in ∃x, may express existence of x in formal logic or mathematics".

senses.definition: Univalent.
senses.example: In the reaction, a monadic group bonds to only one other atom, so it cannot form a chain.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the Monas genus of microorganisms.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the monadic organisms swam in tight spirals across the pond sample.

core.definition: Relating to a monad, such as an indivisible unit in Leibniz's philosophy, or to a function or operator taking one argument.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOH-. The second syllable is weak, and the -ic ending is a short 'ik', not 'eek'. Keep the d crisp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. The word carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective mainly in philosophy, logic, and computer science. In math and logic, 'unary' is often more common for one-argument operations, while in functional programming 'monadic' refers to the monad pattern. Outside technical contexts, it sounds unusual.

distinctions.note: Unary is the common term for one-operand operations in math and programming; monadic is more common in logic and functional programming.
Dyadic means taking or involving two arguments or parts; monadic means taking one argument or relating to a single monad.

examples.everyday: My brother, who studies philosophy, joked that his roommate's view of the world was monadic, with every person living in a closed bubble.
examples.professional: The Haskell team is refactoring the parser to use a monadic interface for error handling.
examples.analytical: On Leibniz's view, every monadic substance mirrors the whole universe from its own point of view.

nuance.analogy: Like a room with its own window onto the city: each unit is self-contained but reflects the whole.
nuance.etymology: From monad plus -ic; monad comes from Greek monas 'unit', from monos 'alone'.
common_mistakes: Using monadic in everyday speech where 'single' or 'one-sided' would be clearer.
Confusing monadic with monastic, which has different stress and meaning.

monadic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *μοναδικός* (“single”), from *μονάς* (“a unit”); see *monad*.

senses.definition: The ruler of an absolute monarchy or the head of state of a constitutional monarchy.
A monarch butterfly (Danaus plexippus) and others of genus Danaus, found primarily in North America.
senses.example: Every autumn, thousands of monarch butterflies pass through our town on their way to Mexico.

senses.definition: A stag which has sixteen or more points or tines on its antlers.
senses.example: The hunter could barely believe the monarch he'd spotted at dawn, with sixteen points on his antlers.

senses.definition: The chief or best thing of its kind.
senses.example: Her grandmother's apple pie was the monarch of every church potluck in town.

senses.definition: Any bird of the family Monarchidae.
senses.example: The monarch I photographed in Samoa had a bright orange crest and a sharp call.

core.definition: A king, queen, emperor, or other hereditary ruler who serves as the head of a monarchy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAH-. The second syllable is a weak 'nuhk', and the final -ch is a hard 'k', not 'ch' as in church. The 'ar' before the -ch is reduced to a vowel that ends in r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts. It can sound formal or respectful, but may suggest absolute power when used in political discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monarch mostly in history, news, and discussion of the British royal family, and in school. In everyday talk they often say 'king' or 'queen' instead. The word is also familiar to Americans as the name of the monarch butterfly, which is commonly seen in the United States.

distinctions.note: King is the specific title for a male ruler; monarch is the general term for any hereditary head of state, including queens and emperors.
Sovereign emphasizes supreme authority and independence, and can describe a state as well as a person; monarch refers specifically to the ruling individual.

examples.everyday: We watched the coronation on TV, and my neighbor said the new monarch looked nervous.
examples.professional: In our policy memo we describe the constitutional monarch as a ceremonial head of state with little direct power.
examples.analytical: Hobbes argued that an absolute monarch, with unified authority, was necessary to prevent civil war.

nuance.analogy: Like a captain at the helm of a ship, whose word is final and who passes the wheel to an heir.
nuance.etymology: From Greek monarkhēs 'sole ruler', from monos 'alone' and arkhein 'to rule'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ch as the sound in church; the ending is a hard k.
Confusing monarch with monarchy: the monarch is the person, and the monarchy is the system.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses the Hebrew melek and the Greek basileus for 'king', rather than the word monarch. Key passages: 1 Samuel 8:7 describes the people rejecting God as their king; Psalm 2 presents the LORD's anointed king as a sign of God's rule; 1 Timothy 6:15 calls God the supreme ruler over all earthly kings and lords.

monarch.etymology: From Middle French *monarque*, from Late Latin *monarcha*, from Ancient Greek *μονάρχης*, variant of *μόναρχος* (“sole ruler”), from *μόνος* (“only”) + *ἀρχός* (“leader”), equivalent to.

senses.definition: Synonym of moral obligation.
senses.example: Reporting the safety violation was a moral duty, not just a matter of company policy.

core.definition: An action one is morally bound to perform because it is right, whether or not the law or a contract requires it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DUTY, and moral has a secondary stress with a reduced ending. Pronounce the r in moral clearly, and make the final y in duty a clear long e sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes something admirable, though it can sound heavy or preachy if used too often.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use moral duty in conversations about personal ethics, public responsibility, and speeches, as in I felt it was my moral duty to speak up. It sounds a little more formal or weighty than moral obligation, which is nearly identical in meaning. In everyday talk, people often use it to explain why they did something difficult.

distinctions.note: The two are nearly synonymous, but duty sounds more personal and heavier, while obligation can also describe social or contractual commitments.
A legal duty is required by law and enforced by courts, while a moral duty binds conscience even when no law requires it.
Responsibility emphasizes accountability for an outcome, while moral duty emphasizes what one ought to do.

examples.everyday: I felt it was my moral duty to tell my sister the truth about the car, even though it was awkward.
examples.professional: We have a moral duty to disclose the error to customers, even though the contract does not require it.
examples.analytical: Kant grounds moral duty in the rational will rather than in consequences or inclination.

nuance.analogy: A moral duty is like a debt you owe to your own conscience, and no court needs to collect it for you to feel bound to pay.
nuance.etymology: Moral comes from Latin moralis; duty comes from Anglo-French deuté, from due, owed.
common_mistakes: Using moral duty to mean any job responsibility, when it specifically refers to ethical obligation.
Confusing duty with due, which is related but a different word in modern English.

senses.definition: In a morbid manner, or to a morbid degree.
senses.example: She joked morbidly about her own funeral, which made the whole dinner table uncomfortable.

core.definition: In an unhealthy way, with strong interest in death, disease or disaster; or to an extreme and unhealthy degree.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOR. The second syllable has a short i sound, as in 'bit', and the final -ly is 'lee'. Do not stress the second syllable as 'bi-DLY'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually implies an unhealthy fascination or an excessive quality that others find disturbing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'morbidly curious' or 'morbidly fascinated' about gruesome news, true crime or disasters, usually in a joking or mildly disapproving way. 'Morbidly obese' is a medical term that can sound blunt or clinical, so avoid it in casual conversation about a person. In everyday speech, 'a little morbid' is a common and gentle way to say that something is grim.

distinctions.note: Macabre describes things that are grim or horrifying, like a story or decoration, while morbidly describes a person's unhealthy attitude or a degree of excess.
Morbidity is a medical or statistical word for the rate of disease, so it is not used for a person's mental attitude.

examples.everyday: My kids are morbidly curious about the shark documentary, so we ended up watching the whole thing.
examples.professional: The retrospective dwelt morbidly on every failed deployment, so the team stopped speaking up in meetings.
examples.analytical: Some medieval memento mori art is read as morbidly fixated on death, though its makers intended it as a call to repentance.

nuance.analogy: Morbidly is like turning up the volume on a grim topic until it becomes unhealthy, the way a small hobby can become an obsession.
nuance.etymology: From Latin morbidus, diseased, from morbus, disease.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'mor-BID-lee'.
Confusing morbidly with morbidity, which is a medical rate and not an adverb describing attitude.

senses.definition: A set of moral norms or customs derived from generally accepted practices rather than written laws.
senses.example: Many of the town's mores, such as neighbors helping at harvest, were never written into any law.

core.definition: The customs and moral standards that a particular society or group takes for granted as right and proper.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable rhymes with 'days'. The word is a plural noun, but Americans use it with singular verbs in many contexts, though it is usually treated as plural.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Mores is used mainly in sociology, history, ethics, and formal writing when describing a group's unwritten rules. Americans say it in serious discussion about cultural change, such as shifting social mores. In casual speech, people more often say customs, values, or norms.

distinctions.note: Norms is more general and often used in social science; mores implies deeper moral weight and is more closely tied to what is considered right.
Laws are written and enforced by the state; mores are unwritten and enforced by social approval or disapproval.

examples.everyday: Some of the old dating mores in our town seem strange to my kids now.
examples.professional: Our HR training covers the workplace mores that new hires may not know, such as how to address senior staff.
examples.analytical: Durkheim argues that a society's mores are internalized through education and ritual, which makes them more binding than law.

nuance.analogy: Mores are like the unwritten house rules of a whole society: nobody posted them on the fridge, but everyone knows when someone breaks one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin mores, plural of mos, meaning custom or manner.
common_mistakes: Using mores as a singular noun, as in 'a more' for one rule.
Confusing mores with the comparative 'more' in pronunciation or meaning.

mores.etymology: From Latin *mōrēs* (“ways, character, morals”), the plural of *mōs*.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being moribund.

core.definition: The state of being near death or near an end, with little chance of recovery or revival.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress shifts from the first syllable of the adjective moribund (MOR-ih-bund) to the third syllable of the noun, so say mor-ih-BUN-dih-tee. The final syllables are reduced to a short uh-tee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests decline, decay or failure, and it can describe institutions, hopes or relationships as well as living things.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, bookish word. Americans would normally say dying, failing, or on its last legs in everyday talk, and reserve moribundity for news analysis, essays or literary description, such as a declining company or a stalled project. Don't use it for an ordinary illness or a temporary slowdown.

distinctions.note: Mortality is the general condition of being subject to death, while moribundity is the state of being at or near the point of ending.
Decline is a neutral, general word for a gradual drop in strength or value, while moribundity suggests that an end is close.

collocations: the moribundity of the old system

examples.everyday: Honestly, the whole downtown feels like it's in moribundity since the big mall closed.
examples.professional: Our legacy reporting pipeline is in a state of moribundity, so we should plan its replacement this quarter.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the moribundity of the old liberal consensus reveals not its failure but its exhaustion.

nuance.analogy: Like a candle that has burned almost to the end of its wick, flickering but unable to recover.
nuance.etymology: From Latin moribundus, 'dying', from morī, 'to die'.
common_mistakes: Using it for a mild illness or a temporary setback, since it implies that something is near its end.
Confusing it with mortality, which names the general fact of being mortal rather than a state close to death.

senses.definition: Situated or occurring on the summit of a mountain.
senses.example: The mountaintop monastery is reached only by a narrow path that winds through pine forest.

senses.definition: The summit of a mountain.

core.definition: The highest point or summit of a mountain; the top of a mountain, often used for views or as a place of special experience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the second part top with the vowel of cot, not caught. The middle syllable of mountain is weak.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests height, clarity, achievement or a moment of insight, and it can also be used literally.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say mountaintop for both literal and figurative meanings, such as a mountaintop view or a mountaintop experience. Mountaintop removal is a technical mining term used in environmental discussions. In everyday talk, Americans often say top of the mountain or summit when they want a simpler word.

distinctions.note: Summit is the more formal or technical word for the top of a mountain, while mountaintop is the more common everyday word.
A peak is a single pointed top, while mountaintop can describe the wider top area.

examples.everyday: We hiked all morning, and the mountaintop view was worth every step.
examples.professional: The network tower is on the mountaintop, so the engineers schedule maintenance during calm weather.
examples.analytical: In Exodus, the mountaintop is a place where human beings encounter the holy, and the descent back to the people is equally significant.

nuance.analogy: A mountaintop is like the high platform of a tower: from there, everything below looks clearer and smaller.
nuance.etymology: Compound of mountain and top, from Old English mountain and top.
common_mistakes: Using mountaintop as a verb, when it is only a noun or adjective.
Pronouncing top with the vowel of caught, when Americans use the vowel of cot.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture often places important events on mountains. The Greek word for mountain is oros (ὄρος), and the Hebrew word is har (הר). Matthew 17:1 describes Jesus taking Peter, James and John up a high mountain, where his appearance is changed. Exodus 19:20 describes the LORD coming down to the top of Mount Sinai to meet Moses.

senses.definition: Computation using more than one processor.

core.definition: Running a program or computing task on two or more processors or CPU cores at the same time to finish work faster.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress is on MUL, with a weaker secondary stress on prah. Many learners stress the -ces- syllable of process; in this word the -cess- is a short, unstressed sess, and the -ing ending is a short ing sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers, system administrators, and data scientists use this word most often, for example when a Python script uses several processes to speed up a job. Americans also use parallel processing for the general idea, but multiprocessing usually refers to a specific technique where separate processes each have their own memory. Non-technical people rarely use the word.

distinctions.note: Multiprocessing runs separate processes that each have their own memory, while multithreading runs several threads inside one process that share memory.
Parallel processing is the general idea of doing work at the same time; multiprocessing is one specific way to do it using multiple processes.
Concurrency means tasks can overlap in time, even on one processor; multiprocessing achieves true simultaneous execution on several processors.

examples.everyday: My new laptop handles multiprocessing so well that the fan almost never turns on while I edit photos.
examples.professional: We cut the preprocessing time in half by moving the feature extraction step to multiprocessing across all sixteen cores.
examples.analytical: Multiprocessing sidesteps the global interpreter lock in CPython, which is why it helps CPU-bound work where threads alone do not.

nuance.analogy: Like hiring several cooks for one kitchen, each with their own stove and ingredients, instead of one cook who moves between pans.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from Latin multi-, 'many', and process, from Latin processus, 'a going forward'.
common_mistakes: Confusing multiprocessing with multithreading, which is a different technique with shared memory.
Stressing the -ces- syllable, as in mul-tih-prah-SESS-ing; the main stress is on the first syllable.

core.definition: A person who feels responsible for the well-being of others, especially those in need. The phrase comes from Cain's question in the Bible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BRUH and KEE. The 'th' in 'brother' is voiced, as in 'the,' and the final 'er' is a reduced American r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing care for others, but can be negative when used to reject responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in sermons, speeches, community talk and everyday conversation about helping others. It sounds slightly formal or literary, and it often appears in the negative form 'I am not my brother's keeper' to deny responsibility. Use it with care in mixed company, because many Americans will recognize the biblical source.

distinctions.note: A good Samaritan is a person who helps a stranger in need, while 'my brother's keeper' describes a broader sense of responsibility for others.
'Responsible for' is a plain and neutral phrase, while 'my brother's keeper' carries a moral and religious tone.

examples.everyday: When my friend lost her job, I felt like I had to be her brother's keeper and help her find work.
examples.professional: As a team lead, I see myself as my brother's keeper, so I check in when someone is overloaded.
examples.analytical: Cain's reply in Genesis 4:9 raises the question of whether moral responsibility extends beyond kinship to all neighbors.

nuance.analogy: It is like a shared lifeboat: each person in it is responsible for keeping the others afloat.
nuance.etymology: Derived from the biblical question in Genesis 4:9, in the Revised Standard Version wording 'Am I my brother's keeper?'
common_mistakes: Using 'my brother's keeper' only for a sibling; the phrase refers to any fellow human being.
Confusing 'keeper' with a goalkeeper or zookeeper; here 'keeper' means someone who guards or looks after someone.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind 'keeper' is shomer, meaning guard or watchman, from the root shamar, meaning to keep, guard or watch. In Genesis 4:9 Cain responds to God's question about Abel with 'Am I my brother's keeper?', which is a question that denies responsibility and hides his guilt. God answers by hearing Abel's blood crying from the ground in Genesis 4:10, which shows that Abel's fate matters to God. Genesis 4:12 then shows the consequences for Cain, who becomes a fugitive and wanderer.

senses.definition: Creation of any myth.

core.definition: The creation of myths, especially new mythic stories written as literature, rather than the study of existing myths.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the pee syllable, and the word ends in an unstressed uh sound, not a long ee. Do not pronounce the poe as poh; the letters oe are pronounced ee here.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it sounds scholarly and is often used with admiration for a writer's imaginative power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mythopoeia almost only in literary criticism, theology and academic writing, often about fantasy writers such as J. R. R. Tolkien or C. S. Lewis. In everyday speech people would say making up myths or creating a mythology. The word is rare, so use it in writing or in a serious discussion of literature.

distinctions.note: Mythology is a body of myths belonging to a culture, while mythopoeia is the process of making myths.
Mythopoetic is the adjective describing things that show or involve this process, while mythopoeia is the noun naming the process itself.

examples.everyday: My friend who writes fantasy novels says she loves the process of mythopoeia, because she gets to invent gods and their stories from scratch.
examples.professional: In our creative writing workshop, we discussed mythopoeia as a way to build a believable world with its own history and beliefs.
examples.analytical: Tolkien's theory of mythopoeia holds that myth-making is a creative act that reflects a deeper truth about human imagination and the world.

nuance.analogy: If mythology is a finished house, mythopoeia is the act of building it, with each beam and wall added by a human hand.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mythopoiia, myth-making, from mythos, story, and poiein, to make.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the oe as oh, as in mith-oh-POY-uh; the correct vowel is ee.
Using mythopoeia to mean a particular myth rather than the act of creating myths.

mythopoeia.etymology: From *mytho* + *poeia*, dated 1846 CE, based on Ancient Greek *μυθοποιία* (“myth-making”).

senses.definition: (archaic) Either directly or indirectly preceded or followed by an auxiliary verb, often must: of necessity or need; necessarily, indispensably.
senses.example: Whatever the weather, the farmer must needs ride out to the far fields.
senses.label: archaic

senses.definition: Plural of need.
Third-person singular simple present indicative of need.

core.definition: Of necessity; necessarily. Used almost only in 'must needs' and 'needs must.'

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a long EE vowel and a final z sound, so it sounds like NEEDZ. The d is quick and does not form a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral but old-fashioned; it can sound quaint, playful, or elevated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use needs as an adverb outside the set phrases 'must needs' and 'needs must.' These appear in literature, sermons, and playful speech, and in casual talk they can sound stiff or humorous. The normal modern phrase is 'have to' or 'must.'

distinctions.note: The verb needs means requires, as in 'he needs help'; the adverb appears only in fixed phrases like 'must needs.'
Necessarily is the everyday adverb for something inevitable or required, while needs sounds archaic and literary.

examples.everyday: The roof is leaking, so we must needs call somebody this week, I guess.
examples.professional: The schedule slipped, so we must needs reduce the scope of the pilot.
examples.analytical: If God is good, then evil must needs be the absence of good rather than an equal rival.

nuance.analogy: Like an old coat in the back closet: it still fits the occasion, but few people wear it outside formal or literary settings.
nuance.etymology: From Old English nēdes, the genitive of need, used adverbially.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I needs to go' for 'I need to go'; needs is the third-person verb, and with I or you you use need.
Using needs as a general adverb, as in 'it needs be done'; say 'it must be done' instead.

needs.etymology: From Middle English *nedes* (“of necessity, necessarily; inevitably, unavoidably”), from Old English *nēdes*, *nīedes* (“of necessity; not willingly”), from *nīed* + *-es*.

senses.definition: A proposition which is the contradictory of another proposition and which can be obtained from that other proposition by the appropriately placed addition, or insertion, of the word "not". (Or, in symbolic logic, by prepending that proposition with the symbol for the logical operator "not".)
senses.example: In logic class, the negation of 'every student passed' is 'at least one student failed.'

senses.definition: The logical operation which obtains such (negated) propositions.
senses.example: Our data pipeline applies negation to the filter mask before joining the two tables.

senses.definition: The act of negating something.
senses.example: Her steady negation of every rumor eventually made the gossip die out.

senses.definition: A denial or contradiction.
senses.example: The senator's negation of the accusations did little to calm the angry voters.

senses.definition: A negative particle; a word, particularly an adverb, with a negative meaning: for instance, no and not in English, nōn, haud and nē in Latin, οὐ and μή in ancient Greek.
senses.example: In Ancient Greek class, we learned that negation before a participle usually takes the particle mē.

core.definition: In logic, a statement that says the opposite of another statement, often formed by adding 'not'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'GAY', and the final syllable 'shun' is reduced to a syllabic n, so it is 'nih-GAY-shn'. Don't pronounce a full vowel after the sh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term in logic, mathematics, and linguistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'negation' mainly in logic, mathematics, grammar, and philosophy classes, and it is standard in those fields. In everyday talk the word is rare; people say 'the opposite' or 'not'. In grammar, 'negation' refers to words like 'not' and 'never' that make a sentence negative.

distinctions.note: 'Negative' is a general adjective, while 'negation' is the logical or grammatical operation of making something negative.
'Denial' is a social or emotional refusal to accept a fact, while 'negation' is a neutral logical operation.

examples.everyday: My kid's English homework was about negation, so we practiced making sentences with 'not' and 'never'.
examples.professional: In the SQL query, the negation of the condition excludes every row where the status is active.
examples.analytical: In classical logic, the negation of a proposition is true exactly when the proposition is false, which is the basis of proof by contradiction.

nuance.analogy: Negation is like a mirror in logic: it flips a statement to its opposite while keeping its structure.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'negatio', from 'negare', meaning to deny or say no.
common_mistakes: Using 'negation' in everyday conversation where 'the opposite' would be more natural.
Confusing 'negation' with 'negative'; the noun names the operation, while the adjective describes the result.
patterns: [U, C] the negation of a statement

negation.etymology: From Middle English *negacioun*, from Old French *negacion*, from Latin *negātiō* (“a denial; negative word”).

senses.definition: Within a topological space:
Within a metric space:
The infinitesimal open set of all points that may be reached directly from a given point.
senses.example: In the discrete model, each point's neighborhood contains only the points reachable in one infinitesimal step.

senses.definition: The set of all the vertices adjacent to a given vertex.
senses.example: In a social network graph, the neighborhood of a user includes all friends directly connected to them.

senses.definition: The residential area near one's home.
senses.example: He lives in my neighborhood.

senses.definition: The inhabitants of a residential area.
senses.example: The fire alarmed the neighborhood.

senses.definition: A formal or informal division of a municipality or region.
senses.example: We have just moved to a pleasant neighborhood.

senses.definition: An approximate amount.
senses.example: He must be making in the neighborhood of $200,000 per year.

senses.definition: The quality of physical proximity.
senses.example: The slums and the palace were in awful neighborhood.

senses.definition: A set containing an open set which contains some specified point.
senses.example: In the proof, we need a neighborhood of x that excludes the sequence's tail.

senses.definition: Alternatively: An open set which contains some specified point.
senses.example: For continuity at p, we must find a neighborhood of p that maps inside the target set.

senses.definition: A set containing an open ball which contains a specified point.
senses.example: Every point in the interval has a neighborhood formed by a small open ball.

senses.definition: Alternatively: An open ball which contains some specified point.
senses.example: Within this neighborhood of radius one, the function values stay close to zero.

senses.definition: The set of all cells near a given cell used to determine that cell's state in the next generation.
senses.example: In a cellular automaton, each cell's neighborhood determines its state in the next generation.

senses.definition: (dated) Close proximity; nearness.
senses.example: The old farmhouse sat in such close neighborhood to the river that floods reached its porch.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A local area within a town or city, or the people who live there.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a quick, weak 'bur,' and the final 'hood' rhymes with 'good.'

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting community and familiarity, though it can imply safety or danger depending on the area.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use neighborhood constantly for local areas, such as 'a quiet neighborhood' or 'what's the neighborhood like?' It can describe a specific area of a city, a suburb, or a group of neighbors. In math, the word has a precise technical meaning.

distinctions.note: Community emphasizes shared identity or interests and may not be geographic, while neighborhood is a specific local area.
A district is an official or administrative area, while a neighborhood is an informal, lived-in area.

examples.everyday: We moved to a quieter neighborhood near the park, and the kids can ride bikes on the sidewalk.
examples.professional: The data team is mapping service requests by neighborhood to find where response times are longest.
examples.analytical: In a metric space, a neighborhood of a point is an open set containing that point, which lets us define limits without fixing a distance.

nuance.analogy: A neighborhood is like a ring of nearby houses around your own: everything you can reach easily from your front door.
nuance.etymology: From neighbor plus -hood, a suffix meaning 'condition or group,' so 'the state of being neighbors.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as a full 'bor' rather than a weak 'bur.'
Using neighborhood to mean a single house; it refers to a wider area.

neighborhood.etymology: From an alteration of earlier *neighborred* (“neighborhood”), from Middle English *neȝeburredde*, *neheborreden*, equivalent to *neighbor* + *red*; the term being interpreted as *neighbor* + *-hood*.

conversation.text: Is this a safe neighborhood to walk around at night?
Our neighborhood has a great bakery and a park.
Slow down; this is a neighborhood with lots of kids.

senses.definition: Synonym of nouveau riche.
senses.example: The neo-rich developers bought up the old warehouses and built glass condos.

core.definition: People who have recently become wealthy and who show off their money in ways others consider tasteless or lacking refinement.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'rich', which ends in a 'ch' sound, like 'itch'. The first word 'neo' is NEE-oh. Do not say 'reach' for the second word.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests showy spending and a lack of social polish, and it can sound snobbish if used casually.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say 'neo-rich'. They usually say 'new money' in casual talk, or 'nouveau riche' in more formal writing. Using 'neo-rich' may sound like a rare or invented variant, so it is best to choose one of the more common phrases. The term is always mildly judgmental about people's taste.

distinctions.note: Nouveau riche is the standard phrase, and it is more widely recognized, while neo-rich is a rare synonym with the same meaning.
New money is the everyday American phrase, and it is less formal and often less insulting than nouveau riche.

examples.everyday: Their new house has gold faucets and a giant fountain, which my dad says is very neo-rich.
examples.professional: We should avoid marketing that looks condescending toward neo-rich buyers who are simply new to premium products.
examples.analytical: Veblen's theory of conspicuous consumption helps explain how the neo-rich display wealth as a bid for social recognition.

nuance.analogy: The neo-rich are like someone who buys the most expensive car on the lot and drives it with the sticker still on, to make sure everyone sees the price.
nuance.etymology: From Greek neos (new) and English rich, from Old English ric (powerful, wealthy).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'nouveau riche' as 'nuvo reech' with a long ee instead of the American 'NOO-voh REESH'.
Using 'neo-rich' in ordinary conversation when 'new money' sounds more natural to Americans.

senses.definition: A value investing technique developed by Benjamin Graham in which a company is valued based solely on its net current assets.
senses.example: Graham's net-net strategy screens for stocks trading below their net current assets.

senses.definition: Get to the point; stop rambling; show me the bottom line.
senses.example: Net-net, we're over budget, so we need to cut the marketing spend now.

core.definition: The final, simplified bottom line of a discussion or analysis, stated after all details and qualifications are set aside.

pronunciation.tip: Both syllables use the same short e. The stress usually falls on the second word, net-NET, though NET-net is also heard in casual speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly jargony. It sounds efficient in business meetings but can seem like insider talk if used outside work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'net-net' in business meetings, emails, and planning talks to get to the conclusion, as in 'So, net-net, we need the budget approved by Friday.' It is informal and belongs in spoken business talk rather than formal reports. In finance, the term also refers to a value investing method developed by Benjamin Graham, but that meaning is much less common in everyday speech. A natural reply is 'Got it, so what's the net-net?'

distinctions.note: Bottom line is the more widely understood phrase and works in both formal and casual speech, while net-net is mostly used in business settings.
Net by itself refers to what remains after deductions, while net-net refers to the final point in a discussion.

examples.everyday: I know you had a long week, but what's the net-net on the car repair, is it going to cost a lot?
examples.professional: Thanks for the detailed deck; net-net, we should move the launch to next month and staff up the support team.
examples.analytical: Stripped of its caveats, the paper's net-net is that the model improves accuracy only when the training data is clean.

nuance.analogy: Net-net is like the final score of a game rather than the play-by-play: it tells you who won without every move.
nuance.etymology: Business slang built on net in the sense of 'final, after all adjustments'; the exact origin of the doubled form is unclear.
common_mistakes: Using net-net in formal writing, where a clearer phrase like 'in summary' fits better.
Writing 'nett-nett' or leaving out the hyphen.

senses.definition: The state of being niggardly; parsimony.

core.definition: The quality of being stingy or unwilling to spend, give, or share generously.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NIG, and reduce the -erd to a quick r-colored vowel. The ending -ness is a soft, short sound, not a long ess.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes stinginess, often in a formal or moral way.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, formal word that Americans would normally replace with stinginess or tightness. Because it contains the sound of a racial slur, many speakers avoid it aloud, even though the word has a separate origin. It appears mostly in writing, especially in literary or policy criticism.

distinctions.note: Stinginess is the common, neutral word for refusing to spend or give; niggardliness is more formal and rarer.

examples.everyday: Her niggardliness with the office coffee budget annoys everyone on the team.
examples.professional: The niggardliness of the training budget made it hard to keep our engineers current.
examples.analytical: The niggardliness of the welfare provisions reflected a moral judgment about deserving and undeserving citizens, not merely a fiscal constraint.

nuance.analogy: Niggardliness is like a faucet that drips only when you need water, holding back what could flow freely.
nuance.etymology: Formed from niggardly, from Middle English nigard, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable or lengthening the middle vowels; it is NIG-erd-lih-nuss.
Using niggardliness in speech where stinginess sounds more natural.

senses.definition: The ordinal form of the number ninety-eight, describing a person or thing in position number 98 of a sequence.
senses.example: The answer appears on the ninety-eighth page of the book.

senses.definition: One of ninety-eight equal parts of a whole.
senses.example: A ninety-eighth of 1960 is 20.

core.definition: The ordinal form of ninety-eight; coming in position number 98 in a sequence.

pronunciation.tip: Put primary stress on EIGHTH and a lighter stress on NINE. In fast speech the t in eighth is often dropped, so the word sounds like 'AYTH'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is used for dates, floors, sequence numbers, and versions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ninety-eighth in plain counting, such as a numbered floor, a version, or a rank. In writing, the ordinal is usually spelled out in full or shown as 98th. People often just say 'ninety-eight' in casual speech when a precise order is not needed.

distinctions.note: Ninety-eighth is position 98 and ninety-ninth is position 99; the two are easy to confuse on lists.

examples.everyday: Our hotel room is on the ninety-eighth floor, so the view of the city is amazing.
examples.professional: The ninety-eighth build failed the regression tests again, so we need to check the dependency update.
examples.analytical: The ninety-eighth verse of the chapter marks a shift from lament toward hope, and that shift shapes the whole argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a row of seats in a theater: the ninety-eighth seat is one specific place in a long line.
nuance.etymology: From ninety-eight plus the ordinal suffix -th, using the root of eight from Old English eahta.
common_mistakes: Writing 'ninety-eight' when the ordinal is needed; the correct form is ninety-eighth.
Dropping the final th sound, which makes it sound like 'ninety-eight' in speech.

senses.definition: Said in response to an obvious statement.
senses.example: Person A: The Cleveland Browns are not doing too awful well this year.

senses.definition: An exclamation of amazement.

core.definition: An informal exclamation meaning you agree strongly, or that you are surprised or impressed by what someone said.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KID, and the -ing ending is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'ing' rather than 'eeng'. Link the two words smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to lighthearted; it can express agreement, sarcasm, or real surprise depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say it casually among friends or colleagues, often as 'No kidding!' to show that an obvious point is obvious or that a surprise is genuine. Tone matters: said flatly after an obvious statement, it can sound sarcastic. Avoid it in formal settings.

distinctions.note: Really? asks for confirmation; no kidding expresses agreement or surprise and does not expect an answer.
You don't say is a little more ironic and older-sounding; no kidding is more casual and common.

examples.everyday: It's supposed to hit ninety degrees today. No kidding, it's brutal out there.
examples.professional: The migration failed twice before it worked. No kidding, we were all surprised.
examples.analytical: When a conclusion is trivially obvious, the reply no kidding can reveal how little the speaker expected of the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like saying 'you think?' with a grin: it confirms the obvious with a little humor.
common_mistakes: Using it as a literal question about kids, which confuses learners; it means 'really' or 'I agree'.
Using it in formal writing or serious discussion, where it sounds too casual.

conversation.text: "It's really hot today." "No kidding. It's like a hundred degrees."
"I used to live in your building." "No kidding! Which floor?"
"This line is long." "No kidding. We've been here forever."

senses.definition: Synonym of noiseless.

core.definition: Free of unwanted sound or random interference, so that a signal, recording or measurement is clean.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, NOISE, as in most compound adjectives, and say the second part with a clear American r. The 'oy' in noise is a diphthong like the one in 'boy'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests clarity, precision and good quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term most often in engineering, audio, data science and telecommunications, where it describes clean signals or data. In everyday talk, people more often say 'quiet' for a place, and they might use 'noise-free' when they want to stress a total absence of disturbance. The hyphen is usually kept before a noun, as in 'a noise-free room'.

distinctions.note: 'Noise-free' is more common in technical contexts and measurement. 'Noiseless' is more general and sometimes more literary.
'Quiet' describes a low sound level in a place. 'Noise-free' means no unwanted signal or disturbance at all, which is a stronger technical claim.

examples.everyday: The hotel room was nice and noise-free, so we actually got some sleep before the wedding.
examples.professional: We need a noise-free dataset before we train the model, or the results will be unreliable.
examples.analytical: Many theoretical results assume a noise-free channel, a condition that real communication systems never fully achieve.

nuance.analogy: A noise-free signal is like a radio tuned exactly to one station, with no static between you and the music.
nuance.etymology: 'Noise' from Old French noise, 'outcry, quarrel'; 'free' from Old English frēo, 'not in bondage'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'free' as 'fray' rather than the long 'ee' sound.
Using 'noise-free' for an ordinary quiet room in casual talk, where 'quiet' is more natural.

senses.definition: A competitive strategy in which firms deliberately don't engage in price reductions, but rather compete in advertising, quality, or design etc.

core.definition: Rivalry between firms that competes through quality, advertising, design, or service instead of lowering prices.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TISH, the sh syllable, in competition. Learners often stress the -pe- syllable or say com-pe-TEE-tion, but American speech uses a short i there.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise economic term.
nuance.usage_note: Economists and business writers use non-price competition to describe markets where companies compete on brand, product design, features, service or loyalty programs. In everyday business talk, Americans usually say they compete on quality or service. The term appears mostly in textbooks, analyses and strategy discussions.

distinctions.note: A price war is repeated price cutting; non-price competition is the strategy of avoiding it.
Differentiation is one method of non-price competition; non-price competition is the broader strategy.
Monopolistic competition is a market structure; non-price competition is a strategy that is common within it.

examples.everyday: Those two pizza places don't fight over price much; their competition is all about service and atmosphere, which is non-price competition.
examples.professional: Our marketing team wants to shift from discounts toward non-price competition, focusing on product quality and loyalty programs.
examples.analytical: In markets with differentiated products, non-price competition can be more sustainable than price cutting, which invites retaliation.

nuance.analogy: Like two bakeries on the same street: instead of slashing bread prices, they outdo each other with better pastries, music and service.
nuance.etymology: Combines non- (not), price (from Latin pretium 'value, reward') and competition (from Latin competere 'to strive together').
common_mistakes: Thinking non-price competition means there is no competition; it is still rivalry, just not on price.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying com-pe-TEE-tion instead of com-pe-TISH-un.

senses.definition: Not contradictory.

core.definition: Not containing or involving any contradiction; consistent, so that no statement or part conflicts with another.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on DIK, with a lighter secondary stress on NAHN. The final -ory is reduced to tuh-ree with a clear American r, and the cot-caught merger means the vowels in nahn and kahn sound alike.

nuance.connotation: Positive in logic, philosophy and careful argument; neutral in other contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use noncontradictory mostly in logic, philosophy, law, science and careful writing, when they want to say that a set of claims is consistent. In everyday speech they say 'consistent' or 'makes sense.' Calling a story noncontradictory is a compliment in a formal argument, but in casual talk it can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Consistent is the everyday word for not conflicting; noncontradictory is more precise and used in logic, philosophy and formal argument.
Coherent means logically connected and easy to follow; a text can be coherent yet still contain contradictions, so the two properties differ.

examples.everyday: I'm not trying to argue with you, I just want a story from you that's noncontradictory.
examples.professional: We need a noncontradictory set of requirements before the team starts building anything, or we will keep rewriting the code.
examples.analytical: Some theologians hold that a noncontradictory account of divine attributes is possible, while others treat apparent paradox as central to revelation.

nuance.analogy: A noncontradictory set of claims is like a road map where every sign points the same direction; no sign tells you to go both ways.
nuance.etymology: From non- (not) plus contradictory, from Latin contradicere, to speak against.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on the wrong syllable, as in non-con-TRA-dic-to-ry; the main stress falls on DIK.
Using it for a small difference in wording; it means no statements conflict at all, which is a stricter standard than 'similar'.

senses.definition: Not derived from dairy sources.

core.definition: Made without milk, cream, butter, cheese or other products derived from the milk of dairy animals.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on NAHN, the first syllable, with the second syllable lighter. In dairy the r is clear and the vowel sounds like air, so avoid saying dee-ree.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it is often chosen for health, allergy, ethical or dietary reasons.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nondairy constantly on menus, grocery labels and in cafés, for milk substitutes like oat or almond milk, and for creamers and whipped toppings. Most people say 'dairy-free' in conversation, which sounds stricter. A nondairy creamer may still contain milk-derived ingredients, so people with milk allergies should read the label. At a coffee shop you can simply ask, 'Do you have nondairy milk?'

distinctions.note: Dairy-free suggests no dairy ingredients at all; nondairy on labels sometimes allows milk-derived ingredients such as casein, so check the ingredient list.
Vegan means no animal products at all, including eggs and honey; nondairy refers only to dairy and does not guarantee that a food is vegan.

examples.everyday: Can I get an oat latte with nondairy milk, please?
examples.professional: The catering order needs a nondairy dessert, since two of the guests have milk allergies.
examples.analytical: Labeling a product nondairy is a legal and marketing choice, and it does not always mean the product is free of milk proteins.

nuance.analogy: Calling a product nondairy is like calling a sweater wool-free: it tells you one main ingredient is missing, but not everything else about it.
nuance.etymology: From non- (not) plus dairy, from Middle English deierie, a dairy, from deye, a dairymaid.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on DAIR, as in nahn-DAIR-ee; the main stress is on NAHN.
Assuming nondairy means vegan; the word only excludes dairy, so eggs or honey may still be present.
